      <h1>Team Readiness Scorecard &mdash; Eight Dimensions, Scored Honestly</h1>

      Pack A - Groundwork (pre-work)<br>

    Source: <b>Team Structures for AI-Augmented Delivery</b>, <i>Team Assessment Worksheet</i> &middot;
    <code>handbook/ch06-team-structures.qmd</code> L339-354 &middot;
    <a href="https://danielmeppiel.github.io/agentic-sdlc-handbook/handbook/ch06-team-structures.html#sec-team-assessment">#sec-team-assessment</a>
    &middot; also ch08, ch10, ch27, index
  </div>

  <div class="ws-instruction">
    Turn the sheet over after scoring. Read the bands against the scores on the front, then mark this team's adoption posture. Reassess quarterly through your first year: write the date below.
  </div>

  <div class="ws-block">
    <h2>Interpreting results <span class="ws-block-note">printed by the book &mdash; nothing to fill</span></h2>
    <div class="prior">Three-point key for column 5, derived from the chapter's own bands: 1-2 = Not Ready &middot; 3 = Partially Ready &middot; 4-5 = Ready.<span class="prior-src">derived: ch06 L358-362 &times; ch08 L57-66</span></div>
    <div class="prior"><b>Scores of 1&ndash;2 on any dimension</b> indicate a gap that will actively undermine agentic adoption. Address these before expanding agent usage. Knowledge explicitness and senior presence are the two dimensions that unblock everything else &mdash; if these score low, start there.<span class="prior-src">ch06 L358</span></div>
    <div class="prior"><b>Scores of 3</b> indicate basic capability that will work for pilot-level adoption but will not scale. Plan to invest during the expansion phase described in Chapter 8.<span class="prior-src">ch06 L360</span></div>
    <div class="prior"><b>Scores of 4&ndash;5</b> indicate readiness. These are the dimensions where your team can be a model for others.<span class="prior-src">ch06 L362</span></div>
    <div class="prior"><b>A pattern we frequently observe</b> in early assessments: high marks on senior presence and psychological safety, low marks on knowledge explicitness and context ownership. This is normal. It reflects teams that have strong people and weak infrastructure &mdash; which is exactly what agentic development exposes.<span class="prior-src">ch06 L364</span></div>

    <div class="ws-meta">
      <b>WS-06-team-readiness-scorecard</b><br>
      Pack A - Groundwork (pre-work)<br>

  <div class="ws-source">
    Source: <b>Team Structures for AI-Augmented Delivery</b>, <i>Team Assessment Worksheet</i> &middot;
    <code>handbook/ch06-team-structures.qmd</code> L339-354 &middot;

  <div class="ws-instruction">
    Fill this together, after every team lead has scored privately. Copy each team's scores from its Panel A sheet; name the gap for every team you defer; mark exactly one team as the pilot and get its executive sponsor to sign column 30 in the room. This sheet orders the teams. It does not exclude any of them.
  </div>

  <div class="ws-block">
    <h2>Panel B, part 1 &mdash; rollup and sequencing <span class="ws-block-note">one row per candidate team &middot; no total, no average, no overall grade</span></h2>
    <div class="prior">Rule: teams &ldquo;ready&rdquo; across all dimensions are pilot candidates; teams &ldquo;partially ready&rdquo; in one or two dimensions need targeted investment before they join; teams &ldquo;not ready&rdquo; in codebase or skill readiness need the most preparation and should start last. The assessment is not a gate; it is a sequencing tool.<span class="prior-src">ch08 L53</span></div>
